item.title: Can a 1.7B Model Be an AI Agent? Building a Local Agent with LFM3 + Ollama
item.description:
Imagine running an AI agent on your own computer, without paying for expensive APIs, without sending your data to the cloud, and without a 70-billion-parameter model.

Can a model with just 1.7 billion parameters actually behave like an agent? Can it calculate numbers, check the weather, manage files, save notes and complete several tasks on its own?

That’s the question I set out to test with LFM3, the small model from Liquid AI. I built a complete local agent around it using Ollama, Node.js and React, and then gave it real work. The full walkthrough is on YouTube, and this post covers the same ground in written form.

🎥 Watch the Video

👉 Watch on YouTube: Can a 1.7B Model Be an AI Agent?

The Four Parts

The app has four components:

  1. React frontend. This is where you talk to the agent and watch what it’s doing.
  2. Node.js backend. It talks to the model, handles requests and runs the execution loop.
  3. Ollama. It runs LFM3 locally on your machine.
  4. JavaScript tools. These are the functions the agent can call: a calculator, a weather lookup, file access and notes.

The key idea is the loop between them. The model decides what should happen, the backend executes the operation, and the result goes back to the model.

Tool Calling: The Model Chooses, Your Code Executes

A language model is good at understanding instructions and generating text. On its own, it can’t check live weather, read a file or run a calculation in your app. Tool calling fills that gap.

You give the model a list of tools. Each tool has a name, a description and a set of parameters. When the model needs a calculation, it replies with a structured request, for example:

1
2
3
4

{
  "name": "calculator",
  "arguments": { "expression": "7800 * 0.18" }
}

The model is not doing the math. It is asking the application to run the calculator. The backend checks the arguments, calls the real JavaScript function, and gets back 1404. That result goes to LFM3, which turns it into a normal reply.

The model never gets unrestricted access to your computer. It can only request the tools you have registered.

One Request, Several Tools

Calling one tool is useful. The more interesting case is a single instruction that needs several steps:

Check the weather in Mumbai, calculate 18% GST on 7,800 rupees, save a note about the result, and prepare a summary.

The model works through it in order:

  • Weather: requests the weather tool for current conditions.
  • Calculator: calculates 18% GST, which is 1,404 rupees, for a total of 9,204 rupees.
  • Save note: stores the result.
  • Summary: writes the final answer from the tool results.

The sequence is not hardcoded in the frontend. The model reads the tool descriptions and decides what to call. The backend keeps the loop going, running tools and returning their results, until the model has a final answer. That loop is what separates an agent from a chatbot.

Watching the Agent Think: Live Events and Metrics

I didn’t want a black box where you send a message and wait. The app streams progress to the frontend with Server-Sent Events (SSE). You can see when the request arrives, when LFM3 starts, which tool it selected, when the JavaScript runs, and what came back. If a tool fails, the error shows up in the same timeline.

The dashboard also records performance:

  • Tool execution time, measured around the actual JavaScript function.
  • Time to first token (TTFT), how quickly the model starts answering.
  • Tokens per second, from Ollama’s response metadata.

These numbers come from the running application, not from a demo.

Safety Is Not Optional

Giving an agent tools means controlling what those tools can do. The app uses several guardrails:

  1. Allow-list. The model can only call tools registered in the app.
  2. Argument validation. Arguments must match the tool’s schema before anything runs.
  3. No eval, no arbitrary shell. Maths goes through a dedicated expression parser.
  4. File sandbox. File operations stay inside one workspace folder.
  5. Human approval. Sensitive actions, like deleting a file, pause until a person approves or denies them.

The approval step matters most. An agent should have the minimum permissions it needs, and anything sensitive should stay under human control.

Adding Your Own Tool

Extending the agent means adding a JavaScript function. In the walkthrough I add a roll_dice tool: I register its name, a description, the number of sides as a parameter, and a short implementation that returns a random number from 1 to that count. After restarting the backend, the agent finds the tool in its list. Asking it to “roll a six-sided dice” makes LFM3 pick the tool, supply the argument, and return the JavaScript result.

The model gets a new capability without retraining or changing its architecture. You extend the agent with your own code.

The Real Test

The demo uses one prompt that needs several tools:

Check the weather in Bengaluru, calculate 18% GST on 7,800 rupees, save a note containing the calculation result and today’s date, and prepare a summary.

The agent calls the weather tool, runs the GST calculation, saves the note and then writes a summary. The weather lookup uses an external data source. The model inference runs locally through Ollama.

Performance and Limits

LFM3 is not trying to replace large coding or reasoning models. Here’s what it handles well and where it struggles:

Strengths Limits
Classification Complex reasoning
Structured extraction Tasks that need broad world knowledge
Simple automation Occasionally picks the wrong tool
Lightweight, focused agents Sometimes gives invalid arguments

Tool calling is not perfect every time. That’s why validation, error handling and approval matter. Tool execution and model inference also take very different amounts of time. A calculator finishes almost instantly, while generating a reply takes longer. Watch both.

Takeaways

Can a 1.7-billion-parameter model behave like an agent? Yes, within the right boundaries. It won’t outperform larger models. But you can connect a small local model to your own functions, limit what it can touch, and get real work done.

The pattern in one line:

The model asks for a tool. Your code executes it. The result goes back to the model.

If you want to build something like this, start with one tool, add validation, and only then add more. I’d love to hear what you would build with a local agent. Tell me in the comments on the video.

Thanks for reading, and see you in the next one.

item.title: Liquid LFM3 Explained: Is This the Most Efficient Local AI Model?
item.description:
What if a 1 GB AI model could beat a model more than five times its size?

Not on everything, but on the tasks that matter most for AI agents. That’s exactly what Liquid AI is claiming with LFM3, its new family of small, open-weight models released on October 27, 2026.

In this post, I’ll break down what LFM3 is, how its architecture works, where it wins, where it doesn’t, and who should actually use it.

What Is LFM3?

LFM3 is the third generation of Liquid Foundation Models from Liquid AI. The headline model is LFM3-1.7B, a text model built for local agents and specialised applications.

Spec LFM3-1.7B
Parameters 1.7 billion
Size at 4-bit ~1 GB
Context window 256K tokens
Architecture Tri-hybrid (convolution + attention)
Pre-training data 22 trillion tokens
Weights Open-weight
Developer Liquid AI

To put that size in perspective: at 4-bit precision, the model fits in about one gigabyte, smaller than many mobile games. Yet it supports a 256,000-token context window, enough to hold a small book in memory at once.

It also outperforms Liquid’s previous LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.

Not One Model, a Family of Six

LFM3 isn’t a single model. The first release includes six models, all built from the same base, LFM3-1.7B-Base, and all around the 2-billion-parameter range:

  • Text: for local agents and specialised apps
  • Vision: image understanding
  • Audio: speech and sound input
  • Omni: combines multiple input types
  • Two Decision models: specialised versions of the vision and omni models

Liquid also says every model in the family can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, which makes it practical for developers who want to customise a model for their own use case.

Why Is LFM3 So Fast? The Tri-Hybrid Architecture

Most language models are pure transformers. Every layer uses attention, which gets expensive in both memory and speed as the context grows.

LFM3 takes a different approach that Liquid calls a tri-hybrid architecture. Of its 24 layers:

Layers Type What it does
13 Convolution Fast and lightweight
5 Sliding-window attention Looks only at the nearest 256 tokens
6 Global attention Full attention across the whole context

This mix keeps memory usage low and speed high, especially with long inputs.

What’s clever is how Liquid arrived at this design. They used hardware-in-the-loop architecture search, testing candidates directly on 14 device and backend combinations. These included phones (Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, OnePlus 15), a Raspberry Pi 5, laptops (Apple M4 Max, AMD Ryzen AI), cloud CPUs, GPUs and a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

The result is a model shaped by real-world hardware, not just benchmarks.

LFM3 vs Qwen 3.5 9B: Where It Wins

Liquid compared LFM3-1.7B against several models, including Qwen 3.5 9B, which is more than five times bigger. Here’s where the tiny model comes out ahead:

Benchmark What it tests LFM3-1.7B Qwen 3.5 9B
WebArena-Verified Long tasks in a web browser 38.42 28.94
AutomationBench Tasks inside business apps 41.29 15.10
BFCL V4 Function / tool calling 71.39 62.83
IFEval Instruction following 96.66 92.08
LiveCodeBench v6 Coding problems 73.46 69.86

In simple terms: when it comes to following instructions, calling tools and completing agent-style tasks, LFM3 punches far above its weight. On AutomationBench it scores nearly three times higher than Qwen 3.5 9B.

Where LFM3 Loses: The Honest Comparison

To be fair, and Liquid is upfront about this too, larger models still win on agentic coding and general knowledge:

Benchmark What it tests LFM3-1.7B Qwen 3.5 9B
SWE-bench Verified Fixing real code issues 43.40 51.20
GPQA Diamond Graduate-level science 63.37 80.40
RULER 128K Long-context retrieval 65.56 87.11

This makes sense. A model this small simply can’t store as much world knowledge as one five times its size. LFM3 isn’t a replacement for big models. It’s a different tool for a different job.

Efficiency: LFM3’s Real Superpower

Where LFM3 really shines is efficiency.

Memory for long context. At a full 128K-token context, LFM3 needs just 1.6 GB of KV cache:

Model KV cache at 128K
LFM3-1.7B 1.6 GB
Qwen 3.5 4B 4.3 GB
MiniCPM5 2B 5.6 GB

On-device speed. Measured with llama.cpp at Q4_0 and a 32K context, Liquid reports that LFM3-1.7B decodes 1.8 to 2.8 times faster than the next fastest model tested, while using the least memory.

Server scale. On a single NVIDIA B300 GPU, LFM3 can generate 3.6 billion tokens per day at 1,024 concurrent requests. Liquid even ran more than 300,000 LFM3 agents in parallel to analyse the Enron email archive.

That’s the kind of scale small, efficient models unlock.

Who Should Use LFM3?

LFM3 is a great fit if you:

  • Have an older laptop or limited RAM. It’s one of the most capable models you can run on modest hardware.
  • Are building local AI agents. Its tool-calling and instruction-following scores make it a strong choice.
  • Target phones or edge devices. The architecture was designed on real mobile and edge hardware.
  • Care about privacy. Running locally means your data never leaves your machine.

Chip makers are paying attention too: AMD, Qualcomm and Ambarella all backed the launch, with plans to run LFM3 on their processors.

LFM3 is not the best choice if you need a heavy-duty coding assistant for large codebases or deep factual knowledge. For that, a larger model like Qwen is still the better pick, or use LFM3 alongside one.

Want a bigger local coding model? See Claude Code For Free in VS Code with Ollama + Qwen 3.8.

Final Thoughts: Is LFM3 Worth It?

Verdict
✅ Tiny and fast About 1 GB, with a 256K context window
✅ Great at agents and instructions Beats models 5x its size on these tasks
⚠️ Not for heavy coding or deep knowledge Bigger models still win there

What excites me most is the direction. AI doesn’t have to live in a giant data centre. With models like LFM3, capable AI can run right on your laptop.

What’s Next?

In my next video, I’ll show you how to install and run Liquid LFM3 locally using Ollama and put it to the test with real-world prompts and tasks.

Watch the LFM3 explainer on YouTube and subscribe to The Code Street so you don’t miss the hands-on follow-up.

Would you trust a 1 GB AI model with your daily work, or would you still stick with larger models like Qwen? Let me know in the YouTube comments.

Sources

  • Liquid AI: Introducing LFM3
  • Hugging Face: LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B

All benchmark figures are as published by Liquid AI.
